title: From ICRISAT Lab to Rs 2 Crore Business: The Indian Scientist Behind Edible Spoons
excerpt: Narayana Peesapaty quit crop research to build Bakeys, the Hyderabad startup making cutlery from jowar, rice and wheat that you eat after your meal or let decompose in days.
body:
• Narayana Peesapaty, a former ICRISAT scientist, founded Bakeys Edible Cutlery in Hyderabad in 2010, creating the world's first commercially available edible spoons
  • The cutlery is made from jowar, rice, wheat and black pepper with no preservatives, has a shelf life of over three years and decomposes in four to five days if discarded
  • Bakeys has grown into a Rs 2 crore business, offering spoons in flavours from ginger-cinnamon to carrot-beetroot while promoting millet farming as a water-saving alternative to rice

When Narayana Peesapaty sat down for an in-flight meal years ago and stared at the plastic spoon in his hand, he saw a problem that refused to leave his mind. India produces 33.7 million tonnes of plastic waste daily, and disposable cutlery — used for minutes, lingering in landfills for centuries — is among the most visible culprits.

Peesapaty, then a rural development researcher at the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) in Hyderabad, decided to do something about it. In 2010, he founded Bakeys Edible Cutlery, creating what is widely regarded as the world's first commercially viable edible spoon.

How It Works

The spoons are made from a blend of jowar (sorghum), rice, wheat and black pepper — no preservatives, no artificial colours, no coatings. They are sturdy enough to stir hot soup or tea, hold up for about 20 to 30 minutes of use, and can be eaten after the meal like a dry biscuit.

If discarded, they decompose naturally within four to five days, becoming food for insects and small animals. The contrast with conventional plastic cutlery, which can take 200 to 500 years to break down, is stark.

"We know plastic has got so many chemical complexes that cause cancer, they don't biodegrade, but still we are using a whole lot of plastic disposable cutlery," Peesapaty told The Better India. "We have an alternative now."

The product carries a shelf life of more than three years, a detail that matters for commercial viability and export potential.

The Millet Mission

Peesapaty's choice of jowar as the primary ingredient was deliberate and rooted in his agricultural background. About one-third of India's farmland is devoted to rice, a crop that places enormous strain on the country's groundwater. Millet, by contrast, requires roughly 60 times less water to grow.

By creating commercial demand for jowar through edible cutlery, Peesapaty aims to incentivise farmers to shift away from water-intensive rice cultivation. It is an environmental two-for-one: less plastic waste and more sustainable farming.

"My goal was not only to replace plastic cutlery but also to create a bigger market for millets and encourage farmers to grow more such crops instead of rice," he said.

""We know plastic has got so many chemical complexes that cause cancer, they don't biodegrade, but still we are using a whole lot of plastic disposable cutlery," Peesapaty told The Better India."

Building the Business

Starting Bakeys was not straightforward. The technology for mass-producing edible cutlery did not exist, and Peesapaty used his flat as collateral to secure a bank loan. An early Kickstarter campaign that aimed to raise $20,000 ended up collecting 12 times that amount, signalling global appetite for the concept.

The business has since grown to Rs 2 crore in annual revenue. Bakeys offers spoons in a range of flavours including sugar, ginger-cinnamon, ginger-garlic, celery, black pepper, cumin, mint-ginger and carrot-beetroot. The company primarily sells to caterers, restaurants and ice cream parlours.

Pricing remains the central challenge. A single Bakeys spoon costs roughly Rs 2 to Rs 3, compared with a fraction of a paisa for its plastic equivalent. Peesapaty argues the gap will narrow as production scales. "The cost of edible cutlery can also come down as production increases," he said. "If the demand grows, I plan to buy raw materials directly from farmers, which will reduce costs."

A Growing Market

Bakeys is not alone in the edible cutlery space any longer. Trishula, a Gujarat-based venture founded by Kruvil Patel, makes edible spoons from wheat, salt and water and has grown to a Rs 5 crore business. EdiblePRO, started by two former IBM engineers in Bengaluru, uses millets, pulses and spices to produce a range of edible tableware including plates, bowls and cups, with the Defence Food Research Laboratory assisting in formulation.

The sector has attracted attention from sustainability-focused investors and food delivery platforms grappling with the environmental cost of single-use packaging. With India's food delivery market generating over 100 million orders a month, each accompanied by plastic cutlery and containers, the addressable market is enormous.

For the Indian diaspora, the story carries a particular resonance. It combines Indian scientific ingenuity with a global sustainability challenge, and offers a model of frugal innovation — solving problems with affordable, locally sourced materials — that India is increasingly known for exporting to the world.
